topic: AgentRun: A DSL That Turns Agent Chains Into Deterministic Workflows

key_points: LangChain frames the market as 'Temporal executes your workflows, LangGraph builds your agents' — a durable-execution layer vs an agent-native orchestration framework.

Comparison table sells agent-native features AgentRun does not provide: streaming (SSE/token), built-in short+long-term memory, human-in-the-loop via a single interrupt() call, 30+ production API endpoints, A2A/MCP/Agent Protocol, Studio/Agent IDE.
Attacks Temporal's AI-agent fit: no prompt/context-window concept, no LLM observability or evals, custom signal handlers for HITL, 2MB gRPC payload cap.
Frames the choice as 'many teams run both' — durability stays with Temporal, agent reasoning with LangGraph.
Names the two paradigms directly: deterministic DAGs (LLM only as a transform at defined nodes) vs probabilistic autonomous loops (LLM as orchestrator until it decides the task is done).
Deterministic pros: predictability, debuggability, guaranteed termination, SLA/regulatory compliance. Cons: brittleness on unhandled inputs.
Probabilistic pros: resilience and adaptability. Cons: unpredictable latency, infinite-loop risk, execution paths that make traditional unit testing nearly impossible.
Verdict matches AgentRun's positioning: 'industry consensus for 2026 is hybrid' — deterministic macro-transitions with probabilistic micro-actions, plus iteration/token budgets as guardrails.
Includes a comparison table on control flow, error handling, auditability, and adaptability — a reusable frame for the AgentRun review.

The sharpest definition in the SERP: 'an agentic workflow is a system where a developer wrote the graph and the LLM fills in the nodes; an AI agent is a system where the LLM draws the next edge of the graph at runtime.'
Traces the definition to Anthropic's Building Effective Agents (Dec 2024) and notes Microsoft/OpenAI/LangChain/Google ADK converged on it.
Adds a governance hook: CSIS (Jan 2026) warned definitional ambiguity in 'agentic' procurement undermines governance frameworks.
Cites Gartner's >40% agentic-project cancellation by 2027 and argues risk factors hit hardest when control flow is left open-ended.
Four-term taxonomy table (AI workflow / agentic workflow / AI agent / agentic AI) — useful to place AgentRun precisely on the 'developer draws the graph' side.
Closest philosophical competitor: a graph-first DSL compiled to a canonical IR, with 'compile-once / run-many' execution as the core economic argument.
States the same problem AgentRun targets: prompt-loop orchestration causes rising token cost, hidden state, degraded predictability, weak auditability.
Frames orchestration as 'energy consumption pattern design' — model inference is budgeted explicitly instead of paid implicitly.
Broader emitter story than AgentRun: FastAPI, React/TypeScript, Prisma, OpenAPI, Docker, cron, MCP (ainl-mcp), optional LSP, sandbox/AVM policy generation.
Direct-competitor benchmark for scope: AgentRun stops at the workflow document + host adapters; AINL tries to emit deployable targets.
atman (Rust, MIT/Apache, v1.1.1 Jul 2026) is a flow DSL with an explicit comparison table: 'LLM-driven (model decides tool use)' mainstream agents vs 'Flow-driven (code decides, LLM executes)'.
Claims deterministic, replayable event traces and arbitrary subflow isolation as differentiators.
Shows the same 'deterministic orchestration over agents' thesis is being implemented across ecosystems (Rust here, TypeScript in AgentRun), which supports the trend angle.
Scope-limiting contract example: flows can statically limit what each flow may touch — a capability AgentRun leaves to host adapters.
AgentSPEX (arXiv 2604.13346, Apr 2026) is the academic version of the same idea: a declarative, human-readable DSL for agent systems with specification, verification, and logging.
Ships a visual editor with synchronized graph and workflow views for authoring and inspection.
Evaluated on 7 benchmarks plus a user study claiming better interpretability and accessibility than a popular existing agent framework.
Useful citation to argue the DSL pattern is not a single vendor's idea but a research-backed convergence.

stats.fact: Five prereleases shipped in three days: 0.1.0-beta.1 through beta.5 between 2026-09-23 and 2026-09-26; npm 'latest' still points at beta.4 while 'beta' points at beta.5.
Incumbent orchestration scale for comparison: LangGraph 42,550 stars, Mastra 28,467, Temporal 23,397, trigger.dev 16,450, Dagger 16,311, Inngest 5,903, Restate 4,498, DBOS Transact (py) 1,599.
Gartner: over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls.

AgentRun's own trust model, stated in its docs: 'JavaScript runs in the process. Validation can execute probes. Run unknown workflows in a host-controlled isolation boundary.' There is 'no general hard-kill sandbox here' and synchronous JavaScript can block the process.
Durability is explicitly out of scope: 'Checkpoint, memo, and recovery interfaces are host hooks, not a bundled durable scheduler', and idempotency keys 'do not confer exactly-once delivery'.
Decision confidence is a model output, not calibrated accuracy: 'Confidence is a model output, not an empirically calibrated accuracy guarantee. The demo's 70% threshold is illustrative.'

Typed-decision validation broke on real model output: System One rounded each probability to two places, so about 1% of real eight-option choices summed to 0.99 and were rejected as probability_mass, failing the whole Jev request (fixed in beta.5, issue #25).

Anthropic's definitional axis for the category: workflows are 'systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths'; agents are 'systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage'.

AINL, a competing deterministic-workflow DSL, argues the same economics: use the model to generate a compact graph once, then execute it repeatedly in a deterministic runtime, moving from 'pay-per-run thinking' to compile-once / run-many.

AgentRun ships an authoring loop for agents: the Pi extension's packaged skill builds workflows with the active model, candidates are written to unique directories and never overwrite a draft, and workflowSha256 covers the whole document (including host metadata) for digest comparison.
stats.source: AgentRun README (Pi section), docs/authoring.md, CHANGELOG beta.3/beta.4

angles: The honest framing: AgentRun is not 'deterministic agents', it is deterministic scaffolding around a few probabilistic nodes. Anchor the review on Anthropic's axis (who draws the next edge of the graph) and show where AgentRun sits: developer-authored graph, agent invoked as a node only when investigation is needed.

Cost economics as the actual pitch: the author's HN claim is avoiding 'a full agent loop where one isn't needed'. Note that no published cost or success-rate benchmark exists for AgentRun itself (the demos use scripted fixtures, not live models), so treat the saving as a design argument, not a measured result.

The limits are the story: trusted execution with no hard-kill sandbox, validation that can execute probes, host hooks instead of a durable scheduler, and idempotency keys that do not confer exactly-once. Write this as the practical adoption gate — if your workflow document can come from an untrusted author, AgentRun puts the isolation burden on you.

Durability gap as the real comparison axis with Temporal/Restate/DBOS/Inngest: those give you durable execution; AgentRun gives you an inspectable, versioned workflow document. The honest recommendation is compositional (durable engine underneath, AgentRun document on top) rather than either/or.

Typed decisions as first-class, separately evaluable nodes (judge/gate/verify/sift with confidence thresholds) is the most under-covered differentiator versus graph frameworks. Pair it with the calibration caveat and the beta.5 probability-mass bug to show the gap between 'typed' and 'correct'.

Agent-authored workflows are the genuinely new 2026 angle: the Pi extension lets an agent inspect tools and write the workflow, with an author contract, digest, and host-owned acceptance checks. This turns 'the SOP' into an artifact the agent maintains — the same pattern that shows up in blog-post pipelines and CI harnesses.

Governance hook for commercial intent: tie the pattern to Gartner's >40% cancellation figure and CSIS's definitional-ambiguity warning — determinism is what makes an agent system auditable, testable, and therefore defensible to a risk owner.

Category context, not a single product: atman (Rust), AINL, and AgentSPEX (arXiv) all landed on the same 'code decides, LLM executes' thesis in 2026. AgentRun's specific bet is TypeScript + JSON Schema + Jev typed decisions + Pi authoring, and a deliberate refusal to own the runtime.

Prerelease caution: beta.5 in three days, npm 'latest' lagging at beta.4, API surface still moving under breaking changes between betas. Say plainly that this is production-adjacent, not production-ready, for teams without a host-side isolation and durability story.
